# Mola

> Persistent Linux computers for AI agents. Each machine runs Omarchy, the Arch Linux desktop, in its own virtual machine on the user's own hardware. About one second to create, about seven to become usable. Drive it over REST, MCP, or a persistent low-latency action session.

This file is written for an agent deciding whether to use Mola and then using it.
Every number below is exact. Docs: https://mola.sh/docs/ · Source: https://github.com/obaid/mola-core

## What it is

A local engine (`npx mola-core`) that runs real virtual machines and exposes them
over `http://127.0.0.1:4141`. Not a container, not a cloud service, not a sandbox
emulation. Inside a machine you get root, systemd, pacman, Omarchy's full
Hyprland desktop, a browser, and a real screen at 1280x800 rendered in
software.

Machines are copy-on-write clones of one base image, which is why creating one
costs about a second rather than a 16 GB copy. Machines share nothing after
creation. The engine binds to loopback only; no account, no hosted service in the
middle.

## When to use it

Use Mola when the work needs a **whole computer** rather than a process:

- **Running code you do not trust.** Anything generated, downloaded, or supplied
  by a third party. A machine is disposable and isolated from the user's files.
- **Graphical work.** Anything that needs a browser you can see, a GUI editor, a
  desktop app, or a screenshot. You can look at the screen and click on it.
- **Installing things.** Root, `pacman -S`, system services, kernel modules,
  anything that would pollute the user's machine or needs privileges a container
  will not give you.
- **A clean environment per task.** Reproducing a bug, testing an installer,
  checking that a README's instructions actually work on a fresh system.
- **Long or destructive experiments.** If the machine ends up broken, delete it
  and make another. Nothing is precious.
- **Showing a human what you did.** `open_desktop` returns a URL they can watch
  and take the mouse in.

Do **not** reach for Mola when:

- A shell command on the user's own machine is enough and safe. Creating a VM to
  run `ls` wastes about eight seconds and 4 GB.
- You need state to survive past the task. Machines are disposable by design.
  Stopping one keeps its disk; deleting it does not.
- The host has no hypervisor. macOS needs Apple Silicon and `brew install qemu`;
  Linux needs a working `/dev/kvm`. Most cloud VMs do not expose nested
  virtualisation, so this usually will not run inside another VM.
- The user has not started the engine. It is theirs to run, not yours to install.

## How to use it

### Option 1 — MCP (no code)

If you are an MCP client (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf), the
engine ships a server. The user adds it once:

```sh
npx mola-core                                   # terminal 1, leave running
claude mcp add mola -- npx -y mola-core mcp     # or the equivalent config
```

Seventeen tools become available:

| Group | Tools |
|---|---|
| Machines | `create_machine`, `list_machines`, `start_machine`, `stop_machine`, `delete_machine` |
| Shell | `run_command`, `start_task`, `check_task` |
| Files | `read_file`, `write_file` |
| Screen | `screenshot`, `click`, `move_mouse`, `scroll`, `type_text`, `press_key`, `open_desktop` |

`screenshot` returns a real image, so you can see the desktop and act on what is
there.

### Option 2 — REST API (you write the calls)

Every request under `/v1` needs `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. The token is
printed when the engine starts and stored at `~/.mola/token`.

```sh
export API=http://127.0.0.1:4141/v1
export TOKEN=$(cat ~/.mola/token)

# create; returns { "data": { "id": ..., "status": "booting" } }
curl -s -X POST $API/machines -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"name":"scratch"}'

# poll until status is "ready", usually 6-10 seconds
curl -s $API/machines/$ID -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

# run something
curl -s -X POST $API/machines/$ID/actions -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"action":"exec","command":"grep PRETTY /etc/os-release"}'

# destroy it and its disk
curl -s -X DELETE $API/machines/$ID -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

Endpoints: `GET /v1` · `GET /health` · `POST /v1/machines` · `GET /v1/machines` ·
`GET /v1/machines/{id}` · `POST /v1/machines/{id}/start` ·
`POST /v1/machines/{id}/stop` · `POST /v1/machines/{id}/actions` ·
`POST /v1/machines/{id}/session` · `POST /v1/machines/{id}/tunnels` ·
`POST /v1/machines/{id}/desktop` · `DELETE /v1/machines/{id}`

Nine actions, all to `POST /v1/machines/{id}/actions`, one per request:
`exec`, `read_file`, `write_file`, `screenshot`, `click`, `move`, `scroll`,
`type`, `key`.

### Option 3 — persistent action session

For high-frequency work, mint a single-use WebSocket ticket:

```sh
curl -s -X POST $API/machines/$ID/session \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

Connect to `data.session_url` within 60 seconds. Send uniquely identified JSON
requests such as `{"id":"1","op":"action","action":{"action":"exec","command":"uname -a"}}`.
Mola executes them in arrival order. The socket supports binary file and
screenshot responses plus changed-screen subscriptions up to 10 FPS. A stop,
restart, restore, or delete revokes the connection; obtain a new ticket after
every boot.

File reads and incoming binary writes are limited to 1 MiB. Screenshot frames
may be larger and announce their exact byte length and SHA-256 digest first.

### Option 4 — machine-scoped port tunnel

`POST /v1/machines/{id}/tunnels` with `{"port":9222}` returns a single-use
WebSocket URL carrying binary data to that port on the selected computer's
loopback interface. Use it for native protocols such as Chromium CDP. Callers
cannot select a host, and privileged or Mola-managed ports are refused.

### Option 5 — the chat app

`npx mola-agent` opens a local chat UI with the desktop beside the conversation.
For humans who want to watch, not for you to call.

## Facts that change how you should behave

**`exec` stops at 120 seconds.** Every package install, build, or large download
exceeds it. Detach instead, then poll:

```sh
setsid nohup sh -c 'sudo pacman -Sy --noconfirm neovim' > /tmp/job.log 2>&1 < /dev/null &
echo $! > /tmp/job.pid
# later: check if alive, and read the tail
if kill -0 "$(cat /tmp/job.pid)" 2>/dev/null; then echo RUNNING; else echo FINISHED; fi; tail -40 /tmp/job.log
```

Over MCP this is `start_task` / `check_task` and it is done for you.

**Prefer the shell to the screen.** Anything a terminal can do is faster, cheaper
and far more reliable through `exec` than by clicking. Drive the desktop only
when the task is genuinely graphical. Do not screenshot to check whether a
command worked; `exec` already told you.

**`ready` is not the same as "the process started".** Four states: `booting`,
`ready`, `stopped`, `unknown`. `ready` means the guest daemon has checked in for
this boot and the machine will answer. `unknown` means the runtime cannot see the
machine, which is deliberately not reported as `stopped` — it has not said it
stopped. Wait for `ready` before acting.

**The screen is 1280x800**, and coordinates are in that space with 0,0 top left.
`scroll` acts wherever the pointer already is, so move there first. In Omarchy,
`super-return` opens a terminal, `super-space` the menu, `super-k` the keybinding
list.

**Commands run as `dev`**, who has passwordless sudo. `~` expands in the guest.

**Machines cost real memory.** Defaults are 4 vCPU, 4096 MB, 40 GB disk. The
engine allows 2 running machines and 8192 MB between them unless the user raises
`MOLA_MAX_RUNNING` / `MOLA_MAX_MEMORY_MB`. Reuse one machine for a task rather
than creating several, and delete it when done. Stopping keeps the disk; deleting
does not.

**Desktop links expire.** `POST /machines/{id}/desktop` returns a URL that works
once and lasts 60 seconds. Ask for it when the human is ready to look, not in
advance, and ask again if they need another.

**The engine must already be running.** If nothing answers on 4141, say so and
ask the user to run `npx mola-core`. Do not try to install or start it yourself;
it holds their machines and their disks.

**The guest image is cached.** It is fetched once and reused, so machines are
built from whatever was current when the user installed. If the engine reports
a newer image at startup, `npx mola-core start --refresh-image` fetches it.
Existing machines keep their own disks and are unaffected.

**Cleanup.** `npx mola-core uninstall` removes every machine, the guest image,
keys and token, and reports what it freed.

## Environment

`MOLA_HOME` (default `~/.mola`) · `MOLA_PORT` (4141) · `MOLA_API` ·
`MOLA_MAX_RUNNING` (2) · `MOLA_MAX_MEMORY_MB` (8192)

## Requirements

Node 20+. Apple Silicon Mac with `brew install qemu`, Python 3.10+, an SSH
client; or Linux x86_64 with `qemu-system-x86_64` and a usable `/dev/kvm`.
`npx mola-core doctor` reports what is present and names anything missing.
